rows.explainer: Burning fossil fuels also releases fine particles, which kill far more people than the extra heat does. rows.label: Share of a won climate policy that is due to advocacy at all (all groups together)

source.title: Burstein & Linton (2002), The impact of political parties, interest groups, and social movement organizations on public policy, Social Forces 81(2), 381-408
source.note: Burstein & Linton review the studies published 1990-2000 in the main sociology and political-science journals: organisations influence policy in a minority of the cases studied, at most about half (the publisher's page shows a bot check; the finding as the abstract states it). Second reference class: Baumgartner, Berry, Hojnacki, Kimball & Leech (2009), Lobbying and Policy Change (University of Chicago Press), 98 randomly drawn issues lobbied in Washington: most saw no change over four years, and the side with more resources won only somewhat more often.

rows.explainer: When a climate rule, law or tax credit is won, how much of it was the advocates' doing, rather than what governments, industry, events and public opinion would have done anyway at the same time. Every advocacy group behind the win shares this (each model's attribution row gives the charity's part of all groups' resources), and the shared years a won reform counts say how long the win stands before it would have come anyway. From frequency to share: Burstein & Linton find organisations move policy in at most about half the cases studied, and Baumgartner et al. find that change usually doesn't come even when advocates push for it, and that resources predict it only weakly. If advocacy is decisive for about half of the wins it campaigned for and partly so for others, while the government's own agenda and events also had to line up, the advocates' expected share of a won policy is below one half. Our judgment, 30% (10% to 60%).

rows.label: Ozone deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂e emitted as methane

source.title: US EPA (2023), Regulatory Impact Analysis for the final oil and natural gas standards (EPA-452/R-23-013), section 3.6, citing McDuffie et al. (2023); and UNEP and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (2021), Global Methane Assessment

source.quote: $1,800 per ton of methane (95 percent confidence interval: $760–2,800)
source.note: Global Methane Assessment (https://www.unep.org/resources/report/global-methane-assessment-benefits-and-costs-mitigating-methane-emissions): cutting 180 million tonnes of methane a year prevents about 255,000 premature deaths a year from ozone.

rows.explainer: Methane is also the main fuel of ground-level ozone worldwide, which kills people with lung and heart disease within about a decade of the methane's release, wherever it was emitted. Low: McDuffie et al.'s respiratory ozone deaths, valued by EPA at $1,800 per ton of methane, at a US value of a statistical life of about $11 million: 1.6 deaths per 10,000 tonnes of methane, 0.05 per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂e at a warming potential of 29.8 (respiratory deaths only, and below the full count where incomes are lower). Best guess 0.16 per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂e, the middle of the two on a log scale. The climate conversion adds it per tonne of methane (each model's methane_share row × this), valued like other air-pollution deaths and discounted over the years the extra methane stays in the air (climate.methane_lifetime_years): at 4% a year it counts 0.68 of its undiscounted value. rows.label: Years an extra tonne of methane stays in the air (perturbation lifetime)

source.title: IPCC (2021), Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Chapter 7 (Forster et al.), section 7.6.1.1 and Table 7.15
source.page: Section 7.6.1.1; Table 7.15
source.quote: slightly revised since AR5 to be 11.8 ± 1.8 years

rows.explainer: Methane emitted today is broken down in the air over about 12 years: the extra methane falls by about 8% a year. Ground-level ozone follows the methane in the air, so the ozone deaths of a tonne come over those years, and the climate conversion discounts them that way: at the discount rate r their present value is 1 ÷ (1 + ln(1 + r) × 11.8), 0.68 of the undiscounted count at 4%. The deaths are taken in the year of the exposure; a lag from exposure to death (a few years in EPA's cessation lags) would lower them a little more and isn't counted. The range is the IPCC's ±1.8 years.

source.page: 8.SM.11, Equations 8.SM.10 to 8.SM.15
source.note: Derivation (our run of these standard responses): CO₂ airborne fraction 0.2173 + 0.2240 e^(-t/394.4) + 0.2824 e^(-t/36.54) + 0.2763 e^(-t/4.304); temperature response 0.631/8.4 e^(-t/8.4) + 0.429/409.5 e^(-t/409.5) K per W m⁻²; methane decaying over its 11.8-year lifetime (climate.methane_lifetime_years), scaled to equal CO₂'s forcing over 100 years (GWP100); heat deaths taken proportional to the warming, counted to 2300 like Rethink Priorities'. At 4% a year the discount-weighted delay is 60 years for CO₂ (the site's climate_heat_death_delay) and 23 for methane; undiscounted, a methane CO₂e tonne's warming to 2300 is 0.51 of a CO₂ tonne's. rows.explainer: Methane's warming comes early: it peaks about a decade after the methane is released and is mostly gone after a few decades, while CO₂'s lasts for centuries. Like CO₂'s heat deaths ("Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂", 60), methane's are discounted as if they all came this many years after the tonne. Running the IPCC's standard responses of temperature to a pulse of each gas, with heat deaths following the warming, gives 60 years for CO₂ at a 4% discount rate, the same as the site's figure, and 23 for methane. Our judgment, 23 (18 to 30): 20 at a 6% rate, 27 if heat deaths per degree rise over the century, which pushes them later.

source.page: 8.SM.11, Equations 8.SM.10 to 8.SM.15
source.note: Derivation (our run of these standard responses): CO₂ airborne fraction 0.2173 + 0.2240 e^(-t/394.4) + 0.2824 e^(-t/36.54) + 0.2763 e^(-t/4.304); temperature response 0.631/8.4 e^(-t/8.4) + 0.429/409.5 e^(-t/409.5) K per W m⁻²; methane decaying over its 11.8-year lifetime (climate.methane_lifetime_years), scaled to equal CO₂'s forcing over 100 years (GWP100); heat deaths taken proportional to the warming, counted to 2300 like Rethink Priorities'. rows.explainer: Tonnes of methane are stated in CO₂-equivalents at the 100-year warming potential (GWP100), which makes a methane tonne warm as much as a CO₂ tonne over its first 100 years; CO₂ goes on warming for centuries after, and the heat deaths of a tonne of CO₂ are counted to 2300 (Rethink Priorities). source.title: South Coast AQMD (May 2024), Draft Socioeconomic Impact Assessment for Proposed Amended Rule 1146.2 (adopted 7 June 2024)
source.page: Table 2 (annual per-unit gas and electricity demand), p. 10; universe, pp. 2-3; Table 3 (recurring savings by category), p. 12
source.quote: The total PAR 1146.2 universe is comprised of approximately 1,070,000 units, with approximately 710,000 pool heaters, 300,000 instantaneous water heaters, and 60,000 other units.
source.note: Our arithmetic from the regulator's own figures (the staff report gives NOx, 5.6 tons a day, but no CO₂ figure). Gas no longer burned at full implementation: 710,000 pool heaters × 262.8 therms + 300,000 instantaneous water heaters × 177 + 60,000 other units × 3,814 (the mix of Type 1 and 2 water heaters and high-temperature units implied by Table 3's recurring savings over Table 2's per-unit savings: about 71% Type 1 water heaters at 1,432 therms, 25% Type 2 at 9,419, 4% high-temperature units at 7,517-18,838) = 469 million therms, × 0.005306 t CO₂ per therm (EPA GHG Emission Factors Hub, 53.06 kg per MMBtu) = 2.49 million tonnes. Less the added electricity, 2.73 TWh (710,000 × 1,135 kWh + 300,000 × 1,646 + 60,000 × 23,795), at 0.1 t CO₂ per MWh (0.03 to 0.205: Southern California Edison's 453 lb/MWh in eGRID 2020, the staff report's footnote 66, falling to zero by 2045 under SB 100; the tonnes come mostly in 2035-2050) = 0.27 million. Net 2.2 million. Low 1.4 million: the added power met at the margin by gas plants (0.4 t per MWh) until the grid is clean; high 2.5 million: a nearly clean grid and the other units' mix 10% heavier. Combustion CO₂ only: upstream methane is the methane share of the models that count it.

rows.explainer: Rule 1146.2 requires zero-emission (heat-pump) units when about 1.07 million gas-fired pool heaters, large and tankless water heaters, small boilers and process heaters in the Los Angeles basin are replaced, from 2026 in new buildings and 2029-2033 in existing ones, so the cut builds up as old units wear out. Once every unit is replaced: about 2.2 million tonnes of CO₂ a year (1.4 to 2.5), our arithmetic from the district's per-unit energy figures, net of the power the heat pumps draw. Read by every model that counts this win.
